# ☕ Part 2: Core Java Mastery


## 🟢 Beginner's Guide to Core Java

> **🎯 New to Java?** Start here! This section gives you the complete mental model before diving into the Q&A. If you already know Core Java basics, jump straight to Q1.

---

### 🤔 What is Java and Why Learn It?

Java is a **platform-independent, object-oriented programming language** — the backbone of enterprise backends, Android apps, and microservices. It powers LinkedIn, Netflix, Amazon, and most banking systems.

**The "Write Once, Run Anywhere" magic:**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Code["📝 Hello.java\n(your source code)"]
    -->|javac-compiler| Bytecode["📦 Hello.class\n(bytecode — portable format)"]

    Bytecode -->|JVM-on-Windows| Win["🖥️ Runs on Windows"]
    Bytecode -->|JVM-on-Linux| Lin["🐧 Runs on Linux"]
    Bytecode -->|JVM-on-macOS| Mac["🍎 Runs on macOS"]
    Bytecode -->|JVM-on-Android| And["📱 Runs on Android"]

    style Bytecode fill:#000000,stroke:#ffc107
    style Code fill:#000000,stroke:#28a745
```

> 💡 Your `.class` bytecode file is identical everywhere. The JVM on each platform converts it to that machine's native instructions — that's "write once, run anywhere".

---

### 🏗️ Java's 4 Pillars — The OOP Foundation

Every Java interview starts here. These 4 pillars appear in at least 50% of interview questions:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Enc["🔒 1. Encapsulation — Hide the data"]
        E1["private fields\n(only class can access)"] -->|expose-via| E2["public getters/setters\n(controlled access)"]
        E3["Example: BankAccount\n- balance is private\n- getBalance() is public"]
    end

    subgraph Abs["🎭 2. Abstraction — Hide the complexity"]
        A1["interface / abstract class\n defines WHAT, not HOW"] -->|implemented-by| A2["Concrete class\nprovides the HOW"]
        A3["Example: TV Remote\n- you press POWER\n- don't know the circuit"]
    end

    subgraph Inh["🧬 3. Inheritance — Reuse the code"]
        I1["Animal (parent)\n+name +age\n+eat() +sleep()"] -->|extends| I2["Dog (child)\n inherits Animal's fields/methods\n+ bark() (new method)"]
        I3["IS-A relationship:\nDog IS-A Animal ✅"]
    end

    subgraph Poly["🎭 4. Polymorphism — Same name, different behavior"]
        P1["Animal a = new Dog()"] -->|a.speak| P2["Dog's speak():\n'Woof!'"]
        P3["Animal b = new Cat()"] -->|b.speak| P4["Cat's speak():\n'Meow!'"]
        P5["Same variable type (Animal)\nDifferent runtime behavior!"]
    end
```

### ☕ Java Execution Flow — From Code to Output

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as 👨‍💻 Developer
    participant javac as ⚙️ javac (compiler)
    participant ClassLoader as 🔄 ClassLoader
    participant JIT as ⚡ JIT Compiler
    participant CPU as 💻 CPU

    Dev->>javac: 1. Write Hello.java
    javac-->>Dev: 2. Compiles → Hello.class (bytecode)
    Dev->>ClassLoader: 3. Run: java Hello
    ClassLoader->>ClassLoader: 4. Load Hello.class into memory
    ClassLoader->>JIT: 5. Pass bytecode
    JIT->>JIT: 6. Compile hot methods → native code
    JIT->>CPU: 7. Execute native instructions
    CPU-->>Dev: 8. Output: "Hello, World!" 🎉

    Note over javac,JIT: All of this is managed by the JVM — you just write Java!
```

### 🔑 Key Java Vocabulary — Know These Terms Cold

| Term | Plain English Meaning | Quick Code Example |
|-------|-----------------|---------------|
| **Class** | Blueprint / template | `class Dog { String name; }` |
| **Object** | Actual instance of a class | `Dog fido = new Dog()` |
| **Field** | Variable inside a class | `private String name;` |
| **Method** | Function inside a class | `public void bark() { }` |
| **Constructor** | Special method to create an object | `public Dog(String n) { name = n; }` |
| **`this`** | Reference to the current object | `this.name = name;` |
| **`super`** | Reference to the parent class | `super.speak();` |
| **Interface** | Contract: defines what a class MUST do | `interface Flyable { void fly(); }` |
| **Abstract class** | Partial implementation — can't create directly | `abstract class Shape { }` |
| **`extends`** | Inherit from a class | `class Dog extends Animal` |
| **`implements`** | Implement an interface | `class Bird implements Flyable` |
| **Generic `<T>`** | Type-safe parameter placeholder | `List<String>`, `Map<K,V>` |
| **Lambda** | Short anonymous function (Java 8+) | `x -> x * 2` |
| **Stream** | Data processing pipeline (Java 8+) | `list.stream().filter(...).collect(...)` |
| **`final`** | Cannot be changed / overridden | `final int MAX = 100;` |
| **`static`** | Belongs to class, not to objects | `Math.sqrt(4)` |
| **`null`** | No object assigned | `Dog d = null;` |

### 📐 Primitive Types vs Reference Types — The Fundamental Divide

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Prim["📦 Primitive Types — stored on STACK"]
        direction TB
        P1["byte   → 8-|bit| integer  (-|128| to 127)"]
        P2["short  → 16-|bit| integer"]
        P3["int    → 32-|bit| integer (most common)"]
        P4["long   → 64-|bit| integer"]
        P5["float  → 32-|bit| decimal"]
        P6["double → 64-|bit| decimal (most common)"]
        P7["char   → single Unicode character"]
        P8["boolean→ true / false"]
    end

    subgraph Ref["🔗 Reference Types — stored on HEAP"]
        direction TB
        R1["String → sequence of chars"]
        R2["Integer, Long, Double... → wrapper classes"]
        R3["Arrays → int[], String[]"]
        R4["Objects → any class instance"]
        R5["Collections → List, Map, Set..."]
    end

    Prim -->|Autoboxing| Ref
    Ref  -->|Unboxing| Prim
```

```java
// Primitives — hold the VALUE directly
int x = 42;        // x IS 42
int y = x;         // y gets a COPY of 42
y = 100;           // x is still 42!

// References — hold an ADDRESS to an object
Dog fido = new Dog("Fido");   // fido POINTS to a Dog object
Dog buddy = fido;             // buddy points to THE SAME Dog object
buddy.setName("Buddy");       // BOTH fido and buddy see "Buddy" — same object!
```

---

### 🔐 Access Modifiers — Who Can See What?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Levels["Access Level (most restrictive → least restrictive)"]
        direction TB
        PR["🔒 private\nOnly within this class"]
        PK["📦 package-|private| (default)\nThis class + same package"]
        PO["🔓 protected\nThis class + subclasses + same package"]
        PU["🌐 public\nEveryone can access"]
        PR --> PK --> PO --> PU
    end
```

| Modifier | Same Class | Same Package | Subclass | Everywhere |
|-----------|--------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
|`private` | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| *(default)* | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `protected` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| `public` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

> 💡 **Interview rule**: Always use the **most restrictive** access level possible. Start with `private`, open up only when needed.

### 🎯 Beginner Quick-Fire Q&A — Warm Up

**Q: What's the difference between `int` and `Integer`?**
> `int` is a primitive — stores the value directly, fast, no `null`.
> `Integer` is a wrapper class — an object that wraps an `int`, can be `null`, works with Collections.
> Java automatically converts between them (autoboxing/unboxing).

**Q: Can you have more than one constructor in a class?**
> Yes! This is called **constructor overloading**. Each constructor must have different parameters:
> ```java
> class Dog {
>     Dog() { }                          // no-arg constructor
>     Dog(String name) { this.name = name; }  // name constructor
>     Dog(String name, int age) { }     // name+age constructor
> }
> ```

**Q: What is `null` in Java?**
> `null` means "no object". A reference variable holds `null` when it doesn't point to any object.
> Calling a method on a `null` reference throws `NullPointerException` — one of the most common Java bugs!
> ```java
> String s = null;
> s.length(); // 💥 NullPointerException!
> ```

**Q: What is the difference between `==` and `.equals()`?**
> `==` compares memory addresses (are these the SAME object?).
> `.equals()` compares content (do these objects have the SAME VALUE?).
> Always use `.equals()` for Strings and objects!

**Q: What is `static` in Java?**
> `static` means "belongs to the CLASS, not to any specific object".
> Static fields are shared across ALL instances. Static methods can be called without creating an object:
> ```java
> Math.sqrt(16);    // Math is never instantiated — sqrt is static
> Integer.parseInt("42");  // same — no new Integer() needed
> ```

## Q1. JDK vs JRE vs JVM

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Think of it like a **car ecosystem**:
> - **JVM** = The **engine**. It runs the fuel (bytecode) and moves the car.
> - **JRE** = The **full car** (engine + wheels + fuel tank). Everything needed to *drive* (run a Java app).
> - **JDK** = The **car + full workshop** (spanner, diagnostic tools, manual). Everything needed to *build and fix* the car.
>
> 💡 **Rule:** Developers install **JDK**. Production servers only need **JRE** (no dev tools = smaller + more secure).

---

#### 🏗️ Architecture — JDK Contains JRE Contains JVM

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph JDK["📦 JDK — Java Development Kit  (Developers install this)"]
        direction TB

        subgraph DevTools["🛠️ Developer Tools  (only in JDK, NOT in production)"]
            javac["⚙️ javac\nCompiles .java → .class bytecode"]
            javadoc["📄 javadoc\nGenerates HTML API docs"]
            jdb["🐛 jdb\nCommand-|line| debugger"]
            jvisualvm["🖥️ jvisualvm\nVisual profiler — see live threads,\nheap, CPU usage, GC activity"]
            jconsole["📊 jconsole\nJMX-|based| monitoring console"]
            jar["📦 jar\nPack classes into .jar archive"]
        end

        subgraph JRE["🏃 JRE — Java Runtime Environment  (End users install this)"]
            direction TB

            subgraph Libs["📚 Core Class Libraries"]
                java_lang["java.lang\n(String, Integer, Object...)"]
                java_util["java.util\n(List, Map, Collections...)"]
                java_io["java.io / java.nio\n(File, Stream, Channel...)"]
                java_net["java.net\n(Socket, URL, HTTP...)"]
            end

            subgraph JVM["⚙️ JVM — Java Virtual Machine  (The engine)"]
                direction TB
                ClassLoader["🔄 ClassLoader\nLoads .class files into memory"]
                Verifier["🛡️ Bytecode Verifier\nChecks code is safe before running"]
                JIT["⚡ JIT Compiler\nConverts bytecode → native CPU instructions at runtime"]
                GC["🗑️ Garbage Collector\nAutomatically frees unused heap memory"]

                subgraph MemAreas["💾 Runtime Memory Areas"]
                    direction LR
                    Heap["Heap\n(all objects live here)"]
                    Stack["Stack\n(method frames,\nlocal variables)"]
                    MetaSpace["MetaSpace\n(class metadata,\nstatic vars)"]
                    PC["PC Register\n(current instruction\npointer per thread)"]
                end

                ClassLoader --> Verifier --> JIT
                JIT --> GC
                GC --> MemAreas
            end
        end
    end
```

> 🔑 **The relationship**: `JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM`
> - JVM **cannot** run alone — it needs the class libraries from JRE
> - JRE **cannot** compile code — it only runs already-compiled `.class` files
> - JDK has **everything**: compile, run, debug, profile

---

#### 🖥️ What is jvisualvm? (The Visual Profiler)

`jvisualvm` is a **free GUI tool** bundled with the JDK that lets you see **inside a running Java process** — like an X-ray machine for your application.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph App["☕ Your Running Java App — JVM Exposes These (Steps ①–⑤)"]
        direction LR
        Threads["① 🧵 Threads\n(how many, what state)"] --- Heap["② 🗄️ Heap Memory\n(how much used vs free)"] --- CPU["③ 💻 CPU Usage\n(% used by your app)"] --- GCLog["④ 🗑️ GC Activity\n(how often GC runs, pause times)"] --- Classes["⑤ 📦 Loaded Classes\n(how many classes in memory)"]
    end

    jvvm["⑥ 🖥️ jvisualvm\n(GUI Tool on Developer Machine)"]

    App -->|⑥-connects-via-JMX-attach-API| jvvm

    subgraph Panels["📊 jvisualvm — What You See (Steps ⑦–⑬)"]
        direction LR
        P1["⑦ Overview\n(PID, JVM args, system info)"] --- P2["⑧ Monitor\n(live CPU + Heap graph)"] --- P3["⑨ Threads\n(timeline: running/sleeping/waiting)"] --- P4["⑩ Sampler\n(which methods use most CPU/memory)"] --- P5["⑪ Profiler\n(record method call timings)"] --- P6["⑫ Heap Dump\n(snapshot of all objects in heap)"] --- P7["⑬ Thread Dump\n(snapshot of all thread stack traces)"]
    end

    jvvm -->|displays-data-in| Panels
```





**How to launch jvisualvm:**
```bash
# Option 1: From JDK bin folder (bundled with JDK 8, available as separate download for JDK 11+)
jvisualvm

# Option 2: Download standalone VisualVM (same tool, updated versions)
# https://visualvm.github.io/
```

**What each panel tells you (Interview answers!):**

| Panel | What You See | When You Use It |
|--------|-----------------|-----------------|
| **Monitor** | Live graph of Heap used vs total, CPU % | Check if app is consuming too much memory |
| **Threads** | Color timeline: green=running, orange=sleeping, red=waiting/blocked | Debug thread deadlocks or starvation |
| **Heap Dump** | Snapshot of every object in heap right now | Find memory leaks — what objects are taking up space |
| **Thread Dump** | Stack trace of every thread right now | Debug a frozen/hung application |
| **Sampler (CPU)** | Which methods are called most frequently | Find performance bottlenecks (slow code paths) |
| **Sampler (Memory)** | Which objects are allocated most | Find objects causing memory pressure |

---

#### 🔍 Real-World Example: Debugging a Memory Leak with jvisualvm

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as 👨‍💻 Developer
    participant jvvm as 🖥️ jvisualvm
    participant App as ☕ Java App (suspected leak)

    Dev->>jvvm: Open jvisualvm, connect to app PID
    jvvm->>App: Attach via JVM Attach API
    App-->>jvvm: Start streaming metrics

    Dev->>jvvm: Open Monitor tab
    jvvm-->>Dev: Shows Heap graph — memory keeps growing! 📈

    Dev->>jvvm: Click "Heap Dump"
    App-->>jvvm: Takes snapshot of all heap objects

    jvvm-->>Dev: Shows top 10 objects by count/size
    Note over Dev,jvvm: Sees: ArrayList has 2,000,000 String objects!

    Dev->>jvvm: Double-|click| ArrayList → trace to source code
    jvvm-->>Dev: Shows exact class + line number where leak originates

    Note over Dev: Found the bug! A cache was never cleared.
```

#### 📋 JDK Tool Reference Table

| Tool | Full Name | What it does | Use in Interview |
|---|---|---|---|
| `javac` | Java Compiler | Compiles `.java` source → `.class` bytecode | "Compilation step" |
| `java` | JVM Launcher | Runs a compiled Java program | "Execution step" |
| `javadoc` | Doc Generator | Generates HTML API docs from `/** */` comments | "Documentation" |
| `jdb` | Java Debugger | Command-line debugger (set breakpoints, inspect vars) | "CLI debugging" |
| **`jvisualvm`** | **Visual VM** | **GUI profiler: heap, threads, CPU, GC monitoring** | **"Profiling & monitoring"** |
| `jconsole` | JMX Console | Lightweight GUI for JMX monitoring | "JMX monitoring" |
| `jstack` | Stack Dump | Prints all thread stack traces to console | "Diagnosing deadlocks" |
| `jmap` | Memory Map | Prints heap stats or takes heap dump | "Memory analysis" |
| `jstat` | JVM Statistics | Real-time GC, class loading, JIT stats from CLI | "GC monitoring" |
| `jar` | Archive Tool | Packs `.class` files into a `.jar` archive | "Packaging" |

---

**Step-by-step — What happens when you run a Java program:**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as 👨‍💻 Developer
    participant javac as ⚙️ javac (compiler)
    participant JVM as 🔄 JVM

    Dev->>javac: javac Hello.java
    javac-->>Dev: Hello.class (bytecode)

    Dev->>JVM: java Hello
    JVM->>JVM: ClassLoader loads Hello.class
    JVM->>JVM: Bytecode Verifier checks safety
    JVM->>JVM: JIT compiles bytecode → native code
    JVM->>JVM: Execute — Heap/Stack/GC manage memory
    JVM-->>Dev: Program output printed
```

**Architectural reasoning**
- Separating runtime (JRE/JVM) from tooling (JDK) keeps production images smaller.
- The JVM boundary allows different language front-ends (Kotlin, Scala, Groovy) to target the same runtime.

| Component | Stands For | Purpose | Who Needs It |
|---|---|---|---|
| **JVM** | Java Virtual Machine | Runs `.class` bytecode | Runtime only |
| **JRE** | Java Runtime Environment | JVM + Standard Libraries | End users / Prod servers |
| **JDK** | Java Development Kit | JRE + Compiler + Dev Tools | Developers only |

---



## Q2. OOP Principles

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> OOP organises code around **objects** — entities that combine related data (fields) and behaviour (methods).
> - **Encapsulation** = A medicine capsule hides its contents. Your class hides internal data behind public methods.
> - **Abstraction** = A TV remote — you press buttons without knowing the circuit board inside.
> - **Inheritance** = `Dog extends Animal`. Dog IS-A Animal — reuse and extend parent behaviour.
> - **Polymorphism** = Same method name, different behaviour. `speak()` returns "Woof" for Dog, "Meow" for Cat.
>
> 💡 **Tip:** Prefer **composition over inheritance** for flexibility. Inheritance creates tight coupling.

---

#### 🔒 Encapsulation — Protecting Your Data

**Analogy**: An ATM machine — you can withdraw money (public method), but you can't directly reach inside and take cash (private field).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Outside["Outside World"]
        User["👤 User Code"]
    end
    subgraph BankAccount["BankAccount class"]
        subgraph Private["🔒 Private (hidden)"]
            balance["balance = ₹5000"]
            pin["pin = 1234"]
        end
        subgraph Public["🌐 Public (accessible)"]
            deposit["deposit(amount)"]
            withdraw["withdraw(amount)"]
            getBalance["getBalance()"]
        end
    end
    User -->|calls| deposit
    User -->|calls| withdraw
    User -->|calls| getBalance
    deposit & withdraw & getBalance -->|reads-writes| balance
    User -.->|no-access| balance
    User -.->|no-access| pin
```

```java
public class BankAccount {
    private double balance;                           // ❌ outside can't touch this
    private String pin;

    public double getBalance() { return balance; }    // ✅ controlled read
    public void deposit(double amt) {
        if (amt > 0) balance += amt;                  // ✅ business rule enforced
    }
    public void withdraw(double amt) {
        if (amt > 0 && balance >= amt) balance -= amt; // ✅ validation before change
    }
}
// Why? If balance were public, anyone could do: account.balance = -999999 — no validation!
```

---

#### 🎭 Abstraction — What, Not How

**Analogy**: A car's steering wheel. You turn it left — the car turns left. You don't know (or need to know) whether it uses hydraulic steering, electric power steering, or rack-and-pinion. The WHAT is the same; the HOW varies.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Contract["📋 Abstract Interface — defines WHAT"]
        PI["interface PaymentProcessor\n\n+ processPayment(amount)\n+ refund(transactionId)\n+ getStatus(transactionId)"]
    end

    subgraph Impl["⚙️ Concrete Implementations — define HOW"]
        CC["CreditCardProcessor\nprocessPayment → calls Visa API"]
        UPI["UpiProcessor\nprocessPayment → calls UPI gateway"]
        BT["BankTransferProcessor\nprocessPayment → calls NEFT/RTGS"]
    end

    PI -->|implements| CC
    PI -->|implements| UPI
    PI -->|implements| BT

    subgraph Service["Your Service — only knows WHAT"]
        Code["PaymentService\nprocessPayment(processor, amount)\n→ calls processor.processPayment(amount)\n→ doesn't care which implementation!"]
    end

    CC & UPI & BT -->|used-by| Service
```

---

#### 🧬 Inheritance — IS-A Relationship

**Analogy**: A `SavingsAccount` IS-A `BankAccount`. It inherits all of BankAccount's features (balance, deposit, withdraw) and adds its own (interest rate).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Animal["🐾 Animal\n+ name: String\n+ age: int\n+ eat(): void\n+ sleep(): void\n+ speak(): String ← abstract"]

    Animal -->|extends| Dog["🐕 Dog\n+ breed: String\n+ speak() → 'Woof!'\n+ fetch(): void"]
    Animal -->|extends| Cat["🐈 Cat\n+ indoor: boolean\n+ speak() → 'Meow!'\n+ purr(): void"]
    Animal -->|extends| Bird["🦜 Bird\n+ wingspan: double\n+ speak() → 'Tweet!'\n+ fly(): void"]

    subgraph HAS_A["HAS-|A| Relationships (Composition — PREFERRED)"]
        Dog2["Dog"] -->|HAS-A| Collar["Collar\n+ id: String\n+ owner: String"]
        Dog2 -->|HAS-A| Vet["Vet\n+ name: String\n+ clinic: String"]
    end

    style HAS_A fill:#000000,stroke:#4caf50 
```

> 🔑 **IS-A vs HAS-A** — one of the most asked OOP questions:
> - **IS-A** = Inheritance (`Dog extends Animal`) — use when a "Dog is a kind of Animal" makes sense
> - **HAS-A** = Composition (`Dog has a Collar`) — use when ownership/containing makes more sense
> - **Rule**: Prefer **HAS-A** (composition) over IS-A (inheritance) — it's more flexible and testable!

---

#### 🔗 HAS-A Relationship (Composition) — Deep Dive

**Beginner Analogy 🚗**: Think of a **Car**. A Car IS-A Vehicle? ✅ Yes. But a Car also **HAS-A** Engine, **HAS-A** Steering Wheel, **HAS-A** GPS. The Engine is NOT a Car — it's a *part* of a Car. That's composition!

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph IsA["❌ IS-A Inheritance — tight coupling (fragile)"]
        Vehicle["🚗 Vehicle\n+ speed\n+ accelerate()"]
        Car["Car extends Vehicle\n+ numDoors"]
        Truck["Truck extends Vehicle\n+ payload"]
        Vehicle --> Car
        Vehicle --> Truck
    end

    subgraph HasA["✅ HAS-|A| Composition — loose coupling (flexible)"]
        Car2["🚗 Car"]
        Engine["⚙️ Engine\n+ horsepower\n+ start()\n+ stop()"]
        GPS["🗺️ GPS\n+ navigate(dest)"]
        FuelTank["⛽ FuelTank\n+ capacity\n+ refuel()"]
        Car2 -->|owns| Engine
        Car2 -->|owns| GPS
        Car2 -->|owns| FuelTank
    end
```

> 💡 **Key insight**: With composition you can swap `Engine` for an `ElectricMotor` without touching anything else in the Car class. With inheritance, changing the parent risks breaking all children — tight coupling!

**Three Flavours of HAS-A:**

```mermaid
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 0}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    subgraph Composition["🔴 Composition — strong ownership\nChild CANNOT exist without parent"]
        direction LR
        House["🏠 House"] -->|owns| Room["🚪 Room\n(demolished with House)"]
    end

    subgraph Aggregation["🟡 Aggregation — weak ownership\nChild CAN exist independently"]
        direction LR
        Library["📚 Library"] -->|contains| Book["📖 Book\n(Book survives Library closing)"]
    end

    subgraph Dependency["🟢 Dependency — uses temporarily\nPassed as a method parameter"]
        direction LR
        Chef["👨‍🍳 Chef"] -->|uses| Knife["🔪 Knife\n(borrowed, not owned)"]
    end
```

**Full Java Implementation — Car with Engine, GPS, FuelTank:**

```java
// ── STEP 1: Define the PARTS (the "HAS" objects) ─────────────────

class Engine {
    private int horsepower;
    private boolean running;

    public Engine(int horsepower) { this.horsepower = horsepower; }

    public void start() {
        running = true;
        System.out.println("Engine started! " + horsepower + "hp roaring 🔥");
    }
    public void stop() {
        running = false;
        System.out.println("Engine stopped ✅");
    }
    public boolean isRunning() { return running; }
}

class GPS {
    private String currentLocation;
    public GPS(String startLocation) { this.currentLocation = startLocation; }

    public String navigate(String destination) {
        return "📍 Navigating: " + currentLocation + " → " + destination;
    }
}

class FuelTank {
    private double capacity;
    private double currentLevel;

    public FuelTank(double capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.currentLevel = capacity;               // start full
    }
    public void refuel(double litres) {
        currentLevel = Math.min(capacity, currentLevel + litres);
        System.out.println("⛽ Tank: " + currentLevel + "L / " + capacity + "L");
    }
    public double getLevel() { return currentLevel; }
}

// ── STEP 2: Compose the OWNER (Car HAS-A Engine + GPS + FuelTank) ─

class Car {
    private String brand;
    private Engine engine;      // 🔴 Composition — Car creates & owns Engine
    private GPS gps;            // 🔴 Composition — Car creates & owns GPS
    private FuelTank fuelTank;  // 🔴 Composition — Car creates & owns FuelTank

    public Car(String brand, int horsepower, double tankCapacity) {
        this.brand    = brand;
        this.engine   = new Engine(horsepower);     // Car builds its own engine
        this.gps      = new GPS("Delhi");
        this.fuelTank = new FuelTank(tankCapacity);
    }

    // Car DELEGATES to its parts — it doesn't do the work itself
    public void start() {
        if (fuelTank.getLevel() > 0) {
            engine.start();                         // delegate to Engine
            System.out.println(brand + " ready to go! 🚗");
        } else {
            System.out.println("❌ No fuel! Please refuel first.");
        }
    }

    public void stop()                    { engine.stop(); }                // delegate to Engine
    public String navigateTo(String dest) { return gps.navigate(dest); }   // delegate to GPS
    public void refuel(double litres)     { fuelTank.refuel(litres); }     // delegate to FuelTank
}

// ── STEP 3: Use it ───────────────────────────────────────────────

Car myCar = new Car("Toyota Camry", 200, 60.0);
myCar.start();                                       // Engine started! 200hp roaring 🔥
                                                     // Toyota Camry ready to go! 🚗
System.out.println(myCar.navigateTo("Mumbai"));      // 📍 Navigating: Delhi → Mumbai
myCar.refuel(10.0);                                  // ⛽ Tank: 60.0L / 60.0L
myCar.stop();                                        // Engine stopped ✅

// 🔄 POWER OF COMPOSITION: want an electric version?
// Just swap Engine for ElectricMotor — the Car class itself is UNCHANGED!
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph CarObj["🚗 Car object in memory"]
        brand["brand = 'Toyota Camry'"]
        engineRef["engine ref"]
        gpsRef["gps ref"]
        tankRef["fuelTank ref"]
    end
    subgraph Parts["Separate objects on the heap"]
        E["⚙️ Engine\nhorsepower=200\nrunning=false"]
        G["🗺️ GPS\nlocation='Delhi'"]
        F["⛽ FuelTank\ncapacity=60\nlevel=60"]
    end
    engineRef --> E
    gpsRef --> G
    tankRef --> F
```

**IS-A vs HAS-A Decision Guide:**

| Scenario | Relationship | Reason |
|----|---|----|
| `Dog` → `Animal` | **IS-A** ✅ | A dog truly IS a kind of animal |
| `Car` → `Engine` | **HAS-A** ✅ | Engine is a PART of a car |
| `Manager` → `Employee` | **IS-A** ✅ | A manager IS an employee |
| `User` → `Address` | **HAS-A** ✅ | Address is data held by User |
| `Order` → `OrderItems` | **HAS-A** ✅ | Items are parts of an order |
| Java's `Stack extends Vector` | **BAD IS-A** ❌ | Stack is NOT a Vector; exposes wrong methods |

> ⚠️ **Famous Java mistake**: `Stack extends Vector` is a classic IS-A misuse. Because Stack inherits Vector, callers can do `stack.add(0, "x")` — inserting at any position — which completely breaks the LIFO contract. Composition would have hidden those methods and prevented the bug.

---

#### 🎭 Polymorphism — Two Types You MUST Know

> 💡 **Polymorphism** = "many forms" — the same method name behaves differently depending on context.
> Java has **two kinds**:
> - **Compile-time** (Static Polymorphism) = resolved by the **compiler** → **Method Overloading**
> - **Runtime** (Dynamic Polymorphism) = resolved by the **JVM at runtime** → **Method Overriding**

---

##### ⏱️ Compile-Time Polymorphism — Method Overloading

**Analogy**: A vending machine with ONE button labelled "Dispense". Put in ₹10 → gives chocolate. Put in ₹20 → gives crisps. Same button, different behaviour based on **what you give it** — and the machine "knows" at design time which slot to use.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Overloading["Compile-Time Polymorphism — same name, different signatures"]
        direction TB
        Caller["Calculator calc = new Calculator()"]

        Caller -->|add-int-int| M1["add(int a, int b)\n→ returns 8"]
        Caller -->|add-double-double| M2["add(double a, double b)\n→ returns 4.0"]
        Caller -->|add-int-int-int| M3["add(int a, int b, int c)\n→ returns 6"]
        Caller -->|add-String-String| M4["add(String a, String b)\n→ returns Hello World"]

        CompileNote["🔧 COMPILER picks the right method\nbased on argument TYPES and COUNT\nat COMPILE time — before the program even runs"]
    end
    style CompileNote fill:#1a3a5c,stroke:#4fc3f7
```

```java
// ── COMPILE-TIME POLYMORPHISM — Method Overloading ───────────────

class Calculator {

    // Same name "add" — different parameter signatures
    public int add(int a, int b) {
        System.out.println("▶ Called: add(int, int)");
        return a + b;
    }

    public double add(double a, double b) {           // overload: different param types
        System.out.println("▶ Called: add(double, double)");
        return a + b;
    }

    public int add(int a, int b, int c) {             // overload: different param count
        System.out.println("▶ Called: add(int, int, int)");
        return a + b + c;
    }

    public String add(String a, String b) {           // overload: String params
        System.out.println("▶ Called: add(String, String)");
        return a + b;
    }

    // ❌ NOT valid overloading — only return type differs → COMPILE ERROR
    // public double add(int a, int b) { return (double)(a + b); }
}

// ── USAGE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Calculator calc = new Calculator();

System.out.println(calc.add(5, 3));              // ▶ add(int, int)       → 8
System.out.println(calc.add(2.5, 1.5));          // ▶ add(double, double) → 4.0
System.out.println(calc.add(1, 2, 3));           // ▶ add(int, int, int)  → 6
System.out.println(calc.add("Hello", " World")); // ▶ add(String, String) → Hello World

// The compiler decides WHICH add() to call at compile time based on argument types
```

> 🔑 **Rules for Method Overloading:**
> - Methods must have the **same name**
> - Must differ in **parameter type, count, or order**
> - Return type **alone** is NOT enough to overload (compile error)
> - Can exist in the **same class** — no inheritance needed
> - `static` methods CAN be overloaded

---

##### 🏃 Runtime Polymorphism — Method Overriding

**Analogy**: A "play" button on different apps. Press it on Spotify → music plays. Press it on Netflix → video plays. The SAME method call produces DIFFERENT behaviour — decided at **runtime** based on the actual object type.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Code as Your Code
    participant JVM as JVM (decides at RUNTIME)
    participant Dog as Dog object
    participant Cat as Cat object

    Note over Code: Animal a = new Dog()
    Note over Code: Animal b = new Cat()

    Code->>JVM: a.speak()
    JVM->>JVM: Actual type of 'a' at runtime? → Dog
    JVM->>Dog: Dog.speak()
    Dog-->>Code: "Woof!" 🐕

    Code->>JVM: b.speak()
    JVM->>JVM: Actual type of 'b' at runtime? → Cat
    JVM->>Cat: Cat.speak()
    Cat-->>Code: "Meow!" 🐈

    Note over JVM: This runtime type lookup = "Dynamic Dispatch" / "Late Binding"
```

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Overriding["Runtime Polymorphism — same signature, different behaviour per subclass"]
        Animal2["abstract class Animal\n+ speak(): String  ← defines CONTRACT"]

        Animal2 -->|extends| Dog2["class Dog\n@Override speak() → Woof"]
        Animal2 -->|extends| Cat2["class Cat\n@Override speak() → Meow"]
        Animal2 -->|extends| Bird2["class Bird\n@Override speak() → Tweet"]

        Ref["Animal ref = new Dog()\nref.speak()"]
        Ref -->|JVM-checks-at-RUNTIME| Dog2
        RuntimeNote["🏃 JVM decides WHICH speak()\nto call at RUNTIME\nbased on actual object type"]
    end
    style RuntimeNote fill:#1a3a5c,stroke:#4caf50
```

```java
// ── RUNTIME POLYMORPHISM — Method Overriding ─────────────────────

abstract class Animal {
    private String name;
    public Animal(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public String getName()    { return name; }

    public abstract String speak();                   // CONTRACT — defines WHAT, not HOW
    public void sleep() { System.out.println(name + " is sleeping 💤"); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    private String breed;
    public Dog(String name, String breed) { super(name); this.breed = breed; }

    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Woof! 🐕"; }     // Dog's HOW
}

class Cat extends Animal {
    public Cat(String name) { super(name); }

    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Meow! 🐈"; }     // Cat's HOW
}

class Bird extends Animal {
    public Bird(String name) { super(name); }

    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Tweet! 🦜"; }    // Bird's HOW
}

// ── RUNTIME POLYMORPHISM IN ACTION ───────────────────────────────
List<Animal> shelter = List.of(
    new Dog("Rex", "Labrador"),
    new Cat("Whiskers"),
    new Bird("Tweety"),
    new Dog("Buddy", "Poodle")
);

for (Animal a : shelter) {
    // Reference type = Animal (parent) — but JVM calls the REAL speak() at runtime
    System.out.println(a.getName() + " says: " + a.speak());
}
// Output:
// Rex says:      Woof!  🐕    ← JVM called Dog.speak()
// Whiskers says: Meow!  🐈    ← JVM called Cat.speak()
// Tweety says:   Tweet! 🦜    ← JVM called Bird.speak()
// Buddy says:    Woof!  🐕    ← JVM called Dog.speak()

// ✅ Adding Lion? Zero changes to the loop — just add a new class!
// class Lion extends Animal { @Override public String speak() { return "Roar! 🦁"; } }
```

> 🔑 **Rules for Method Overriding:**
> - Same **method name** and **exact same parameters** (identical signature)
> - Return type must be **same or a subtype** (covariant return)
> - Access modifier must be **same or broader** (`protected` → `public` ✅, `public` → `private` ❌)
> - Always use `@Override` — compiler warns you if the signature doesn't match
> - `static` and `private` methods **cannot** be overridden (they are hidden, not overridden)

---

##### 📊 Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism — Full Comparison

| Feature | ⏱️ Compile-Time (Overloading) | 🏃 Runtime (Overriding) |
|----|---|----|
| **Also called** | Static polymorphism | Dynamic polymorphism |
| **Resolved by** | Compiler | JVM at runtime |
| **Resolved at** | Compile time | Runtime |
| **Method signature** | Must **DIFFER** (type / count) | Must be **IDENTICAL** |
| **Return type** | Can differ | Same or subtype only |
| **Inheritance needed?** | ❌ No — same class is fine | ✅ Yes — parent–child |
| **Annotation** | None | `@Override` (recommended) |
| **Performance** | ⚡ Faster (decided upfront) | Tiny overhead (dynamic dispatch) |
| **Static methods** | ✅ Can be overloaded | ❌ Cannot be overridden (only hidden) |
| **Keyword trigger** | None special | `extends` / `implements` |
| **Classic example** | `print(int)` vs `print(String)` | `Dog.speak()` vs `Cat.speak()` |

```java
// ── SIDE-BY-SIDE MINI EXAMPLE ────────────────────────────────────

// 1️⃣ COMPILE-TIME — same class, DIFFERENT signatures
class Printer {
    public void print(int n)           { System.out.println("Integer: " + n); }
    public void print(String s)        { System.out.println("String: " + s); }
    public void print(int n, String s) { System.out.println("Both: " + n + ", " + s); }
    // Compiler picks at compile time based on what you pass
}

// 2️⃣ RUNTIME — parent-child, SAME signature, different body
class Shape {
    public double area() { return 0; }
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    private double radius;
    public Circle(double r) { this.radius = r; }
    @Override public double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
}
class Rectangle extends Shape {
    private double w, h;
    public Rectangle(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    @Override public double area() { return w * h; }
}

Shape s1 = new Circle(5);        // reference type = Shape (parent)
Shape s2 = new Rectangle(4, 6);  // reference type = Shape (parent)
System.out.println(s1.area());    // 78.53  ← JVM calls Circle.area()    at RUNTIME
System.out.println(s2.area());    // 24.0   ← JVM calls Rectangle.area() at RUNTIME
```

---

**Step-by-step interview walk-through**
1. Encapsulation protects state behind a public API — prevents invalid state.
2. Abstraction hides complexity and exposes only essential contracts — cleaner APIs.
3. Inheritance reuses behaviour where an IS-A relationship makes sense — but use sparingly.
4. Polymorphism lets code depend on interfaces, not concrete classes — easy to extend.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Encapsulation and abstraction reduce coupling between modules.
- Polymorphism enables strategy swaps without changing call sites.
- Prefer **composition over inheritance** — inherit only when the IS-A is truly permanent.

| Pillar | Key Keyword | Interview Trigger Word |
|---------|--------|-----|
| Encapsulation | `private`, `getter/setter`      | "data hiding", "information hiding" |
| Abstraction | `interface`, `abstract`         | "contract", "polymorphic type" |
| Inheritance | `extends`, `super`              | "IS-A", "code reuse" |
| Polymorphism | `@Override`, dynamic dispatch   | "runtime binding", "open/closed" |

---

## Q3. HashMap vs HashTable

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> A **Map** stores key-value pairs — like a phone book. Given any key (name), get its value (phone number) in O(1) average time.

**The Internal Mechanism — How HashMap Actually Works:**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Step1["Step 1: Hash the key"]
        K["Key: 'Alice'"] -->|key-hashCode| H["hashCode = 65198723"]
        H -->|index-eq-hashCode-pct-capacity| Idx["index = 65198723 % 16 = 3"]
    end

    subgraph Step2["Step 2: Store in bucket array"]
        BucketArray["Bucket Array (default size: 16)"]
        B0["[0] → null"]
        B1["[1] → null"]
        B2["[2] → null"]
        B3["[3] → ●"] 
        B4["[4] → null"]
        Bdot["... (to [15])"]
        BucketArray --> B0 & B1 & B2 & B3 & B4 & Bdot
    end

    subgraph Step3["Step 3: Collision handling"]
        B3 -->|linked-list| E1["Entry{key='Alice', value='123-456'}"]
        E1 -->|if-same-bucket| E2["Entry{key='Bob', value='789-000'}\n(different key, same bucket index)"]
        E2 -->|chain-over-8-entries| Tree["🌳 TreeNode\n(O(log n) access)"]
    end

    K --> Step2
    Step1 --> Step2
```

**Step 4 — What happens when HashMap grows (Resize):**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as Your Code
    participant HM as HashMap (capacity=16)
    participant New as New HashMap (capacity=32)

    User->>HM: put("Alice", "123")
    User->>HM: put("Bob", "456")
    Note over HM: ... keep adding entries ...
    User->>HM: put("Zach", "789") (12th entry = 75% full)

    HM->>HM: Load factor exceeded! (0.75 × 16 = 12)
    HM->>New: Create new array (double size: 32)
    HM->>New: Rehash ALL existing entries into new positions
    Note over New: Each key gets a NEW bucket index based on new capacity

    Note over HM,New: ⚠️ Expensive! Pre-|size| your HashMap if you know the expected count
```

```java
// Pre-size to avoid expensive resizes!
// Formula: initialCapacity = (expectedSize / loadFactor) + 1
Map<String, User> users = new HashMap<>(1024, 0.75f); // for ~768 entries

// ✅ Production pattern: ConcurrentHashMap for shared state
Map<String, Integer> wordCount = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
wordCount.merge("java", 1, Integer::sum);  // Atomic read-modify-write

// ✅ LinkedHashMap to preserve insertion order
Map<String, String> ordered = new LinkedHashMap<>();

// ✅ TreeMap for sorted keys
Map<String, String> sorted = new TreeMap<>(); // keys always in sorted order
```

**Step-by-step**
1. A key is hashed and mapped to a bucket index.
2. The bucket stores a single entry or a collision chain.
3. Long chains (>8) are treeified to keep lookups efficient at O(log n).
4. When the load factor (75% by default) is exceeded, the table doubles and rehashes.

**Architectural reasoning**
- O(1) average access depends on good hash distribution and capacity planning.
- Treeification prevents worst-case O(n) behavior when many collisions occur.
- Pre-sizing reduces expensive resize operations on hot paths.

| Feature | `HashMap` | `HashTable` | `ConcurrentHashMap` | `LinkedHashMap` | `TreeMap` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Thread Safety | ❌ No | ✅ Full sync | ✅ Segment locks | ❌ No | ❌ No |
| Null Key | ✅ 1 | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ 1 | ❌ No |
| Null Value | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| Order | ❌ None | ❌ None | ❌ None | ✅ Insertion | ✅ Sorted |
| Performance | ✅ Fastest | ❌ Slowest | ✅ Fast concurrent | Similar | O(log n) |
| Use For | Single-thread | Legacy code | Multi-thread prod | LRU caches | Sorted data |

---

## Q4. ArrayList vs LinkedList

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Both are ordered `List` implementations but differ in how they store elements internally:
> - **ArrayList** = Numbered library shelf. Elements stored contiguously in memory. `get(5)` is O(1) — instant jump to position.
> - **LinkedList** = Treasure hunt chain. Each node holds data + pointer to the next. To reach index 5, traverse 5 nodes = O(n).
>
> 💡 **Default choice:** Always use `ArrayList`. Only pick `LinkedList` for O(1) insertions at both ends (use it as a `Deque`).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph AL["ArrayList — Contiguous Memory Block"]
        direction LR
        A0["[0]\n10"] --- A1["[1]\n20"] --- A2["[2]\n30"] --- A3["[3]\n40"] --- A4["[4]\n50"] --- A5["[5]\n(empty)"]
        Note1["get(3) → direct index jump → O(1) ✅\ninsert at [2] → shift [2],[3],[4] right → O(n) ❌"]
    end

    subgraph LL["LinkedList — Doubly-|Linked| Nodes (scattered in memory)"]
        direction LR
        N1["10\nprev: null\nnext: →"] <--> N2["20\nprev: ←\nnext: →"] <--> N3["30\nprev: ←\nnext: →"] <--> N4["40\nprev: ←\nnext: null"]
        Note2["get(3) → traverse from head: 10→20→30→40 → O(n) ❌\ninsert between nodes → just relink pointers → O(1) ✅"]
    end
```

**Step-by-step**
1. ArrayList stores elements contiguously for O(1) index access.
2. LinkedList stores nodes with pointers; access requires traversal.
3. Inserts in the middle shift ArrayList elements but only relink nodes in LinkedList.

| Operation | ArrayList | LinkedList |
|-----|----|------|
| `get(i)` — random access | **O(1)** ✅ | O(n) ❌ |
| Add at end | O(1) amortised | O(1) |
| Add at start/middle | O(n) ❌ | **O(1)** ✅ |
| Remove from middle | O(n) ❌ | **O(1)** ✅ |
| Memory per element | Low (value only) | High (value + 2 pointers per node) |
| CPU cache performance | ✅ Excellent (contiguous) | ❌ Poor (scattered nodes) |
| Use as Stack/Queue | Possible but not ideal | ✅ Best as Deque |

```java
List<Product> catalog  = new ArrayList<>();   // read-heavy: get(i) is O(1)
Deque<Task>   taskQueue = new LinkedList<>();  // write-heavy: addFirst/removeLast O(1)
```

## Q5. Immutable Class

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> An **immutable** object's state CANNOT change after it is created — like a printed boarding pass.
> - Java's `String` is immutable: `"hello".toUpperCase()` returns a NEW `"HELLO"` string; `"hello"` stays unchanged.
> - **Thread-safe by default:** Multiple threads can read an immutable object with zero locking required.
> - **Safe as HashMap key:** Since `hashCode()` never changes, immutable objects are reliable map keys.
>
> 💡 Use immutable value objects in your domain: `Money`, `Email`, `PhoneNumber`, `ProductId`, `UserId`.

```mermaid
mindmap
  root((Immutable Class Rules))
    final class (no subclassing)
    private + final fields
    no setters / mutators
    deep copy mutable inputs
    return defensive copies
```

**Step-by-step**
1. Make the class `final` and fields `private final`.
2. Avoid setters or any method that mutates state.
3. Deep-copy mutable inputs and return defensive copies.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Immutability simplifies concurrency and caching.
- Immutable objects are safe as map keys and reduce synchronization needs.
- Defensive copying prevents external references from mutating internal state.

```java
public final class Money {                           // Rule 1: final class
    private final BigDecimal amount;                 // Rule 2: private + final
    private final String currency;
    private final List<String> tags;

    public Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency, List<String> tags) {
        this.amount   = amount;
        this.currency = currency;
        this.tags     = new ArrayList<>(tags);       // Rule 4: defensive copy
    }

    public BigDecimal getAmount()  { return amount; }
    public String getCurrency()    { return currency; }
    public List<String> getTags()  {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(tags);   // Rule 5: unmodifiable view
    }

    public Money add(Money other) {                  // Returns NEW object
        return new Money(this.amount.add(other.amount), this.currency, this.tags);
    }
}
// Benefits: Thread-safe by default, safe as HashMap key, cacheable
```

## Q6. String Pool & Performance

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Java maintains a **String Constant Pool** in heap memory. String literals with the same content share one object:
> - `String a = "hello"; String b = "hello";` → both point to the **same** pooled object. `a == b` is `true`.
> - `String c = new String("hello");` → forces a **new** heap object. `c == a` is `false`, but `c.equals(a)` is `true`.
> - `s.intern()` manually adds a string to the pool.
>
> 💡 **Performance:** `str = str + i` in a loop creates thousands of temporary objects. Use `StringBuilder` instead.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Heap["Heap Memory"]
    Pool["String Constant Pool"]
    Hello["hello"]
    World["world"]
    Heap --> Pool
    Pool --> Hello
    Pool --> World

    A["String a = hello"] --> Hello
    B["String b = hello"] --> Hello
    C["String c = new String(hello)"] --> Cobj["new heap object"]
    Cobj -.->|content-equals| Hello
```

**Step-by-step**
1. String literals are stored in the String Constant Pool.
2. Identical literals reference the same pooled object.
3. `new String("hello")` forces a new heap object.
4. `==` compares references; `equals()` compares content.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Pooling reduces memory and speeds up comparisons for repeated literals.
- Avoid `new String(...)` unless you explicitly need a distinct instance.
- Prefer `equals()` for content comparison in production logic.

```java
// ❌ BAD: Creates 10,000 String objects in heap
String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) result += i;  // New object each iteration!

// ✅ GOOD: StringBuilder — single mutable buffer
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(50_000);  // Pre-size for performance
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) sb.append(i);
String res = sb.toString();  // One final String object

// ✅ MODERN: String.join or collectors
String csv = IntStream.range(0, 10_000)
        .mapToObj(Integer::toString)
        .collect(Collectors.joining(","));
```

## Q7. == vs equals()

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Two ways to compare things in Java — they answer different questions:
> - `==` → **Reference equality**: are these two variables pointing to the EXACT SAME object in memory?
> - `equals()` → **Value equality**: do these two objects represent the same logical value?
> - For **primitives** (`int`, `double`, `boolean`), `==` always compares values directly — there are no objects.
> - ⚠️ The `Integer` cache covers -128 to 127: `Integer a=127; a==b` is `true`, but `Integer a=200; a==b` is `false`!
>
> 💡 **Rule:** Always use `.equals()` for Strings and Objects in business logic. Never rely on `==` for Strings.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Stack
        A["a"]
        B["b"]
        C["c"]
    end
    subgraph Heap
        H1["String hello (obj1)"]
        H2["String hello (obj2)"]
    end
    A --> H1
    B --> H1
    C --> H2
```

**Step-by-step**
1. References (`a`, `b`, `c`) live on the stack and point to heap objects.
2. `a` and `b` reference the same heap object → `a == b` is true.
3. `c` references a different object with the same content.
4. `equals()` compares content, not references.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Reference equality (`==`) is fast but only valid when identity matters.
- Use `equals()` for business logic to avoid subtle correctness bugs.
- String interning and caches can affect reference equality; don’t rely on it.

```java
// Primitives: == always compares values
int x = 100, y = 100;
System.out.println(x == y);           // true ✅

        // Integer cache: -128 to 127 are cached!
        Integer a = 127, b = 127;
System.out.println(a == b);           // true (cached!)
        Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(c == d);           // false ❌ (not cached, new objects)
System.out.println(c.equals(d));      // true ✅

// Always override equals() AND hashCode() together!
public class User {
    private final String email;

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof User)) return false;
        return Objects.equals(email, ((User) o).email);
    }

    @Override public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(email);    // Consistent with equals!
    }
}
// Rule: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() MUST be true
```

## Q8. Method Overloading vs Overriding

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Both allow the same method name to serve different purposes:
> - **Overloading** = Same class, same name, **different parameters**. Resolved at **compile time** by the compiler.
    >   Example: `log(String msg)` and `log(String msg, Level level)` — compiler picks the right one based on arguments.
> - **Overriding** = Child class **replaces** the parent's method with its own version. Resolved at **runtime** by actual object type.
    >   Example: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` → calls Dog's `speak()` at runtime even though the variable is typed as `Animal`.
>
> 💡 Always add `@Override` when overriding — the compiler will catch any signature typos immediately.

---

#### 📞 Overloading — Compile-Time Decision

**Analogy**: A phone app with multiple "contact" actions — `call(name)`, `call(number)`, `call(contact, isVideo)`. Same action name ("call"), but compiler picks the right version based on what you pass.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Source["Your Code (compile time)"]
        C1["logger.log('Error!')"]
        C2["logger.log('Error!', Level.ERROR)"]
        C3["logger.log(exception)"]
    end

    subgraph Compiler["⚙️ Compiler — resolves at compile time"]
        Check["Looks at argument TYPES:\n- String only → method 1\n- String + Level → method 2\n- Exception → method 3"]
    end

    subgraph Methods["Logger class methods"]
        M1["void log(String msg)"]
        M2["void log(String msg, Level level)"]
        M3["void log(Exception ex)"]
    end

    C1 --> Compiler --> M1
    C2 --> Compiler --> M2
    C3 --> Compiler --> M3
```

```java
public class Logger {
    // Overloaded methods — same name, different parameters
    public void log(String msg)                         { System.out.println(msg); }
    public void log(String msg, Level level)            { System.out.println("[" + level + "] " + msg); }
    public void log(Exception ex)                       { System.out.println("ERROR: " + ex.getMessage()); }
    public void log(String msg, Object... args)         { System.out.printf(msg + "%n", args); } // varargs

    // ❌ CANNOT overload by return type only — compiler error!
    // public int log(String msg)  ← same name + params as first method = DUPLICATE
}
```

---

#### 🔄 Overriding — Runtime Decision

**Analogy**: A universal remote with a "volume up" button. Each brand (Samsung, Sony, LG) has a different internal implementation of what "volume up" means, but you press the same button.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Code as Your Code
    participant Ref as Animal reference
    participant JVM as JVM (runtime)
    participant Dog as Dog object (actual)
    participant Cat as Cat object (actual)

    Code->>Ref: Animal a = new Dog()
    Note over Ref: variable TYPE = Animal
    Note over Dog: actual OBJECT = Dog

    Code->>Ref: a.speak()
    Ref->>JVM: dispatch speak() call
    JVM->>JVM: Look up actual type: Dog
    JVM->>Dog: Dog.speak()
    Dog-->>Code: "Woof!" ← Dog's version

    Code->>Ref: Animal b = new Cat()
    Code->>Ref: b.speak()
    JVM->>Cat: Cat.speak()
    Cat-->>Code: "Meow!" ← Cat's version

    Note over JVM: This is "Dynamic Method Dispatch" or "Late Binding"
```

```java
class Animal {
    public String speak() { return "..."; }           // base implementation
    public final void breathe() { /* can't override */ } // ← final = no overriding!
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Woof!"; }         // ✅ override — @Override catches typos

    // ❌ CANNOT change to private — would reduce visibility
    // ❌ CANNOT change throws clause to add checked exceptions
}

class Cat extends Animal {
    @Override
    public String speak() { return "Meow!"; }
}

// Runtime polymorphism:
Animal a = new Dog();
System.out.println(a.speak()); // "Woof!" — Dog.speak() called at runtime
```

---

**Full Comparison:**

| Feature | Overloading | Overriding |
|----------|---|-------------|
| **When decided** | Compile time | Runtime |
| **Where** | Same class (or subclass) | Parent → Child class |
| **Method name** | Same | Same |
| **Parameters** | Must differ | Must be identical |
| **Return type** | Can differ | Same OR covariant (subtype) |
| **`@Override`** | Not applicable | Must use (best practice) |
| **Access modifier** | Any | Cannot be more restrictive |
| **`static` methods** | Can overload | Cannot override (hidden, not overridden!) |
| **`private` methods** | Can overload | Cannot override (not inherited) |
| **`final` methods** | Can overload | Cannot override |
| **Constructor** | Can overload | Cannot override |

> ⚠️ **Interview Trap**: Static methods are **hidden**, not **overridden**. If you call a static method through a reference variable, it uses the DECLARED type, not the actual type!
> ```java
> Animal a = new Dog();
> a.speak();          // → Dog.speak() (runtime dispatch — overriding)
> Animal.staticMethod(); // → Animal.staticMethod() (compile-time — hiding, not overriding)
> ```

---

## Q9. Multithreading

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> A **thread** is an independent sequence of instructions inside a process. Multiple threads share the same heap memory.
> - **Single-threaded:** Tasks run one after another. Task A (100ms) + Task B (100ms) = 200ms total.
> - **Multi-threaded:** Tasks run concurrently. Task A and B both run in parallel ≈ 100ms total.
> - **Risks:** Race conditions (two threads corrupt shared data), deadlocks (threads wait for each other forever).
> - **Thread states:** `NEW → RUNNABLE → RUNNING → BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING → TERMINATED`
>
> 💡 **Never** use `new Thread()` in production. Use `ExecutorService` to manage a reusable thread pool.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NEW : new Thread()
    NEW --> RUNNABLE : start()
    RUNNABLE --> RUNNING : scheduled by CPU
    RUNNING --> RUNNABLE : yield()
    RUNNING --> BLOCKED : waiting for monitor lock
    RUNNING --> TIMED_WAITING : sleep()/wait(t)/join(t)
    RUNNING --> WAITING : wait()/join()
    TIMED_WAITING --> RUNNABLE : timeout/notify
    WAITING --> RUNNABLE : notify/lock acquired
    BLOCKED --> RUNNABLE : lock acquired
    RUNNING --> TERMINATED : run() completes
    TERMINATED --> [*]
```

**Step-by-step**
1. `new Thread()` creates the `NEW` state.
2. `start()` transitions to `RUNNABLE` (eligible to run).
3. Scheduler assigns CPU → `RUNNING`.
4. Blocking calls or monitor contention move to `WAITING`, `TIMED_WAITING`, or `BLOCKED`.
5. Notifications or lock acquisition return to `RUNNABLE`.
6. When `run()` finishes, the thread is `TERMINATED`.

**Architectural reasoning**
- State transitions help explain deadlocks, starvation, and latency spikes.
- Understanding `BLOCKED` vs `WAITING` guides which synchronization primitive to change.
- Production tuning focuses on reducing time in `BLOCKED/TIMED_WAITING`.

```java
// ✅ Preferred: Implement Runnable (allows extending other classes)
public class FileProcessor implements Runnable {
    private final String filePath;
    public FileProcessor(String filePath) { this.filePath = filePath; }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Processing: " + filePath
                + " on thread: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}

// Usage with ExecutorService (NEVER use raw Thread in production)
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
executor.submit(new FileProcessor("/data/file1.csv"));
        executor.submit(new FileProcessor("/data/file2.csv"));
        executor.shutdown();
```

---

## Q10. Runnable vs Callable

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Two functional interfaces for defining tasks to run on a thread:
> - **Runnable** = `void run()` — fire and forget. No return value, cannot throw checked exceptions.
> - **Callable<V>** = `V call() throws Exception` — returns a result of type V, can propagate checked exceptions.
> - **Future<V>** = the "receipt" for a Callable's result. `future.get()` blocks until the result is ready (or timeout).
>
> 💡 Modern Java: use `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> ...)` for composable, non-blocking async pipelines.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["Runnable\nvoid run()\nNo return value\nNo checked exceptions\nThread or Executor"]
    C["Callable<V>\nV call() throws Exception\nReturns value\nChecked exceptions\nExecutorService"]
```

**Step-by-step**
1. Use `Runnable` for fire-and-forget work without a return value.
2. Use `Callable` when you need a result or checked exceptions.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Callable enables composition via `Future` and `CompletableFuture`.
- Favor executors for thread management in production.

```java
// Runnable — fire and forget
Runnable emailTask = () -> emailService.send("user@example.com");

// Callable — need result
Callable<UserProfile> profileTask = () ->
        userRepository.findById("user-123")
                .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException("user-123"));

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);

// Submit Callable → get Future
Future<UserProfile>    future  = pool.submit(profileTask);
CompletableFuture<?>   cFuture = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() ->
        userRepository.findById("user-123"));   // Modern approach

try {
UserProfile profile = future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);  // Blocking, timeout
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
        future.cancel(true);  // Cancel if too slow
}
```

---

## Q11. ExecutorService (Production Config)

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Creating a `new Thread()` per request is like hiring a new employee for every customer — expensive. A **thread pool** reuses threads:
> - **Core threads:** Always alive and ready. Pick up tasks immediately.
> - **Work queue:** Holds tasks when all core threads are busy.
> - **Max threads:** Extra threads created if queue overflows. Shut down after idle timeout.
> - **Rejection policy:** What to do when queue AND max threads are full (throw, log, or caller runs).
>
> 💡 **Sizing rule:** I/O-bound tasks → `pool size = CPU cores × 2`. CPU-bound tasks → `pool size = CPU cores + 1`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    In["Incoming Tasks"] --> Core["Core Threads\n(coreSize=10)"]
    Core --> Queue["Work Queue\nLinkedBlockingQueue(1000)"]
    Queue -->|Queue-full| Max["Max Threads\n(maxSize=20)"]
    Max -->|Saturated| Reject["Rejection Handler"]
```

**Step-by-step**
1. Tasks are accepted and executed by core threads first.
2. When cores are busy, tasks are buffered in the work queue.
3. If the queue fills, the pool grows up to `maxSize`.
4. Once both queue and max threads are saturated, the rejection policy applies.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Queue size controls latency vs throughput trade-offs under load.
- Max threads absorb bursts but can increase context switching.
- Rejection policy is a safety valve to prevent cascading failures.

```java
@Configuration
public class ExecutorConfig {

    @Bean("orderProcessor")
    public ExecutorService orderProcessorPool() {
        return new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                10,                              // corePoolSize
                20,                              // maximumPoolSize
                60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,           // keepAliveTime for extra threads
                new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(1_000),// bounded queue — prevents OOM!
                new ThreadFactoryBuilder()
                        .setNameFormat("order-processor-%d")
                        .setDaemon(false).build(),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // Backpressure: caller runs
        );
    }

    @Bean("asyncNotifier")
    public ExecutorService asyncNotifierPool() {
        return Executors.newFixedThreadPool(
                Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() * 2,
                r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "notifier"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; }
        );
    }
}
```

---

## Q12. Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Java exceptions split into two categories based on whether the **compiler forces you to handle them**:
> - **Checked exceptions** (extend `Exception`): Compiler says handle or declare with `throws`. For recoverable situations: file not found, DB unreachable.
> - **Unchecked exceptions** (extend `RuntimeException`): Compiler is silent. For programming bugs: null pointer, array index out of bounds.
> - **Errors** (extend `Error`): JVM-level failures like `OutOfMemoryError`. Do NOT catch these — they're unrecoverable.
>
> 💡 In production Spring Boot: use **custom unchecked exceptions** + `@RestControllerAdvice` global handler for clean code.

```mermaid
mindmap
  root((Throwable))
    Error
      OutOfMemoryError
      StackOverflowError
      VirtualMachineError
    Exception
      Checked Exception
        IOException
        SQLException
        FileNotFoundException
      RuntimeException
        NullPointerException
        IllegalArgumentException
        IllegalStateException
        IndexOutOfBoundsException
        ClassCastException
```

**Step-by-step**
1. All throwable types inherit from `Throwable`.
2. `Error` types signal JVM-level issues; application code typically should not catch them.
3. `Exception` types split into checked (must handle) and runtime (optional).
4. Use checked exceptions for recoverable I/O/DB issues; runtime for programming errors.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Clear exception taxonomy improves error handling consistency in large systems.
- Checked exceptions force callers to make explicit recovery decisions.
- Runtime exceptions simplify APIs but require disciplined validation and testing.

```java
// Checked — compiler forces you to handle
public void readFile(String path) throws IOException {
    try (FileReader fr = new FileReader(path)) { /* process */ }
    // throws IOException if file not found
}

// ✅ Senior Pattern: Custom unchecked for business exceptions
public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String orderId;
    public OrderNotFoundException(String orderId) {
        super("Order not found: " + orderId);
        this.orderId = orderId;
    }
}

// Clean service code — no try/catch pollution
public Order getOrder(String id) {
    return orderRepository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
}

// Global handler catches it
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException ex) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(404)
                .body(new ErrorResponse(404, ex.getMessage()));
    }
}
```

## Q13. Serialization / Deserialization

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> **Serialization** = converting a Java object into bytes so it can be stored (file/DB/cache) or sent over a network.
> **Deserialization** = reconstructing the Java object from those bytes.
> - Mark the class `implements Serializable` and define `serialVersionUID` for version control.
> - Fields marked `transient` are excluded — use this for passwords, DB connections, derived fields.
> - `ObjectOutputStream.writeObject(obj)` serialises; `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` deserialises.
>
> 💡 Modern apps prefer **JSON serialization via Jackson** — language-agnostic, human-readable, easier to version.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Obj["UserSession object\nsessionId, userId, password (transient)"]
    Bytes["Byte stream"]
    Obj -->|serialize| Bytes
    Bytes -->|deserialize| Obj2["UserSession object"]
    Bytes --> File["File (session store)"]
    Bytes --> Net["Network (RMI)"]
    Bytes --> Cache["Cache (Redis)"]
```

**Step-by-step**
1. A Java object is serialized into a byte stream.
2. `transient` fields are excluded from serialization.
3. The byte stream can be stored, transmitted, or cached.
4. Deserialization reconstructs the object from bytes.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Serialization enables persistence and transport across process boundaries.
- `transient` protects sensitive data and prevents accidental leakage.
- Prefer JSON for external APIs; Java serialization is best for internal use cases.

```java
public class UserSession implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;  // Version control!
    private String sessionId;
    private String userId;
    private transient String password;  // transient = NOT serialized ✅
    private LocalDateTime createdAt;
}

// ✅ Modern Production: JSON with Jackson
@Component
public class JsonSerializer {
    private final ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper()
            .registerModule(new JavaTimeModule())
            .disable(SerializationFeature.WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS);

    public String toJson(Object obj) throws JsonProcessingException {
        return mapper.writeValueAsString(obj);
    }

    public <T> T fromJson(String json, Class<T> clazz) throws JsonProcessingException {
        return mapper.readValue(json, clazz);
    }
}
// JSON is language-agnostic, human-readable, versioning-friendly
```

## Q14. Garbage Collection

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> Java manages memory automatically. The **Garbage Collector (GC)** finds objects no longer referenced by anything and frees their memory.
> - You never call `free()` in Java — GC does it, but you must avoid **memory leaks** (unintentionally holding references).
> - **Young Generation (Eden + Survivors):** Where new objects are born. Most die here. **Minor GC** is fast.
> - **Old Generation:** Long-lived objects promoted here. **Major GC** is slow and may cause pause spikes.
> - **GC pause:** The app briefly pauses while GC runs. Modern collectors (ZGC) reduce this to sub-milliseconds.
>
> 💡 **Default (Java 9+):** G1GC. Use **ZGC** for latency-critical services. Always set `-Xms = -Xmx` in production.

---

#### 🔄 Object Lifecycle — Birth to Death

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Your Code
    participant Eden as 🌱 Eden (Young Gen)
    participant S0 as 🔄 Survivor S0
    participant S1 as 🔄 Survivor S1
    participant Old as 🏛️ Old Generation
    participant GC as 🗑️ GC

    App->>Eden: new Object() — object born here
    App->>Eden: new Object() — more objects...
    Note over Eden: Eden fills up!

    GC->>Eden: 🔥 Minor GC triggered
    Eden->>S0: Move SURVIVING objects (age=1)
    GC-->>Eden: Free dead objects ♻️

    Note over S0: Next Minor GC...
    GC->>S0: Minor GC
    S0->>S1: Survivors move, age=2
    Note over S1: Keep surviving...

    GC->>S1: Minor GC — age=|8| (threshold reached)
    S1->>Old: Promote long-|lived| object to Old Gen

    Note over Old: Old Gen fills up!
    GC->>Old: 💥 Major GC (Full GC) — much slower!
    Old-->>GC: Free dead old objects
    Note over App: App pauses during Full GC! Keep it rare.
```

#### 🗑️ Garbage Collector Types — Pick the Right One

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Collectors["GC Collector Comparison"]
        direction TB
        Serial["🐢 SerialGC\nSingle thread\nHigh pause time\nUse for: tiny apps,\nembedded devices"]
        Parallel["⚡ ParallelGC\nMulti-|thread| GC\nHigh throughput\nUse for: batch jobs,\nnon-|interactive| apps"]
        G1["🎯 G1GC (DEFAULT Java 9+)\nRegion-based\nPredictable pauses\n~200ms target\nUse for: most apps\nlarge heaps (4GB+)"]
        ZGC["🚀 ZGC (Java 11+)\nConcurrent\nSub-millisecond pauses\nUse for: latency-critical\n(APIs with <10ms SLA)"]
        Shen["🌿 ShenandoahGC\nConcurrent\nSub-millisecond pauses\nUse for: same as ZGC\n(Red Hat maintained)"]

        Serial --> Parallel --> G1 --> ZGC
        G1 --> Shen
    end
```

#### 🐛 Common Memory Leaks — What to Avoid

```mermaid
mindmap
  root((Memory Leaks in Java))
    Static Collections
      List or Map stored as static field
      Items added but never removed
      Fix: Use WeakReference or clear regularly
    Unclosed Resources
      FileInputStream not closed
      JDBC Connection not closed
      Fix: try-with-resources
    Listeners and Callbacks
      Registered event listener
      Never deregistered
      Fix: Remove listener when done
    ThreadLocal Variables
      ThreadLocal set but never removed
      Thread Pool reuses threads
      Fix: call threadLocal.remove in finally
    Inner Class References
      Non-|static| inner class holds ref to outer
      Outer object cant be GCed
      Fix: Use static inner class
    Caches Without Eviction
      Cache grows forever
      No TTL or size limit
      Fix: Caffeine or Guava with eviction policy
```

```java
// ❌ MEMORY LEAK — cache grows forever!
public class UserService {
    private static final Map<Long, User> cache = new HashMap<>(); // static!

    public User getUser(long id) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(id, userRepository::findById); // never evicts!
    }
}

// ✅ FIXED — Caffeine cache with size limit and TTL
@Bean
public LoadingCache<Long, User> userCache() {
    return Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(1000)                    // max 1000 entries
        .expireAfterWrite(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES) // evict after 10 mins
        .build(id -> userRepository.findById(id));
}

// ✅ ALWAYS use try-with-resources for closeable resources
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(SQL)) {
    // use conn and ps
} // auto-closed even if exception thrown — no memory/connection leak!

// ✅ WeakReference for cache (GC can collect when memory needed)
private final Map<String, WeakReference<HeavyObject>> cache = new WeakHashMap<>();
```

```java
// JVM Production GC Configuration
// -Xms2g -Xmx4g                 → set initial and max heap (keep equal to avoid resize pauses)
// -XX:+UseG1GC                  → G1 collector (Java 9+ default — usually best choice)
// -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200       → G1 targets this pause time (soft goal)
// -XX:+UseZGC                   → ZGC for <1ms pause (Java 11+, production stable in 15+)
// -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log         → Enable GC logging for analysis
// -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError → Dump heap on OOM for analysis
// -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heap.hprof
```

## Q15. Java Streams

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> **Streams** let you process collections of data in a declarative pipeline — like a factory assembly line:
> - **Source:** raw materials — `List`, array, file lines, range (`IntStream.range(0, 100)`)
> - **Intermediate ops (lazy):** machines on the line — `filter()`, `map()`, `flatMap()`, `sorted()`, `distinct()`, `limit()`
> - **Terminal op (eager):** the final output — `collect()`, `count()`, `reduce()`, `forEach()`, `findFirst()`
> - **Lazy evaluation:** nothing runs until a terminal operation is called. This enables short-circuit optimisations.
>
> 💡 Do NOT reuse a stream — after a terminal op, the stream is exhausted. Create a new stream for each pipeline.

---

#### 🏭 Stream Pipeline — The Full Picture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources["📦 Sources"]
        S1["list.stream()"]
        S2["array.stream()"]
        S3["Stream.of(1,2,3)"]
        S4["IntStream.range(0,10)"]
        S5["Files.lines(path)"]
    end

    subgraph Intermediate["⚙️ Intermediate Operations (LAZY — no execution yet!)"]
        direction TB
        filter["filter(predicate)\nKeep elements matching condition"]
        map["map(function)\nTransform each element"]
        flatMap["flatMap(function)\nFlatten nested streams"]
        sorted["sorted() / sorted(comparator)\nSort elements"]
        distinct["distinct()\nRemove duplicates"]
        limit["limit(n)\nTake first n elements"]
        skip["skip(n)\nSkip first n elements"]
        peek["peek(consumer)\nDebug/inspect without modifying"]
    end

    subgraph Terminal["🎯 Terminal Operations (EAGER — triggers execution!)"]
        direction TB
        collect["collect(Collectors.toList())\ncollect(Collectors.groupingBy(...))\ncollect(Collectors.joining(','))"]
        reduce["reduce(0, Integer::sum)\nFold into single value"]
        count["count()\nCount matching elements"]
        findFirst["findFirst() / findAny()\nOptional result"]
        forEach["forEach(consumer)\nPerform action on each"]
        anyMatch["anyMatch() / allMatch() / noneMatch()\nBoolean check"]
        toArray["toArray()\nConvert to array"]
    end

    Sources --> Intermediate --> Terminal
```

#### 🔍 Lazy Evaluation — Why It Matters

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Code as Your Code
    participant Stream as Stream Pipeline
    participant filter as filter(age > 18)
    participant map as map(User::getName)
    participant limit as limit(3)
    participant collect as collect()

    Code->>Stream: list.stream().filter(...).map(...).limit(3).collect(...)
    Note over Stream: Nothing executes yet! Just building pipeline...

    Code->>collect: collect() called — triggers execution!
    collect->>limit: "give me elements"
    limit->>map: "give me elements"
    map->>filter: "give me elements"
    filter-->>map: User(age=25) passes ✅
    map-->>limit: "Alice"
    filter-->>map: User(age=17) filtered ❌
    filter-->>map: User(age=30) passes ✅
    map-->>limit: "Bob"
    filter-->>map: User(age=22) passes ✅
    map-->>limit: "Charlie"
    limit-->>collect: 3 elements found — STOP! (no more processing)
    collect-->>Code: ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]

    Note over filter: ⚡ Short-circuit! Only processed until limit(3) was satisfied
```

```java
// ── COMPLETE STREAM EXAMPLES ────────────────────────────────────────────────

List<Order> orders = getOrders(); // imagine 10,000 orders

// 1. Filter + Map + Collect
List<String> highValueIds = orders.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.getAmount() > 1000)           // only high-value
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == COMPLETED)       // only completed
    .map(Order::getId)                             // extract just ID
    .collect(Collectors.toList());                 // → List<String>

// 2. Group by category
Map<String, List<Order>> byCategory = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::getCategory));

// 3. Count per category
Map<String, Long> countByCategory = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::getCategory, Collectors.counting()));

// 4. Average order amount
OptionalDouble avgAmount = orders.stream()
    .mapToDouble(o -> o.getAmount().doubleValue())
    .average();

// 5. Join names as CSV
String customerNames = orders.stream()
    .map(Order::getCustomerName)
    .distinct()
    .sorted()
    .collect(Collectors.joining(", ")); // "Alice, Bob, Charlie"

// 6. FlatMap — flatten nested collections
List<String> allTags = orders.stream()
    .flatMap(o -> o.getTags().stream())  // Order has List<String> tags
    .distinct()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// 7. Parallel stream — for CPU-intensive work on large collections
long count = orders.parallelStream()               // uses ForkJoinPool
    .filter(o -> expensiveCheck(o))                // runs on multiple threads
    .count();
// ⚠️ Only use parallel for large datasets + stateless operations + no shared state!

// 8. Optional — never return null from streams
Optional<Order> firstBig = orders.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.getAmount() > 10000)
    .findFirst();
// Use: firstBig.ifPresent(o -> process(o));
// Or:  firstBig.orElse(defaultOrder);
// Or:  firstBig.orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException("No big orders"));
```

## Q16. Optional Class

> **🔰 Beginner's Concept**
> `Optional<T>` is a container that **may or may not** contain a non-null value. It makes "this might be null" explicit in the type system.
> - Without Optional: easy to forget null checks → `NullPointerException` at runtime.
> - With Optional: null safety is forced into the API contract — callers must handle the empty case.
> - Key methods: `isPresent()`, `get()`, `orElse(default)`, `orElseThrow()`, `map()`, `filter()`, `ifPresent()`
>
> 💡 Use Optional as **return types only** (not fields or parameters). Never call `optional.get()` without checking first.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Traditional
        T1["getUser(id)"] --> T2["if user != null"] --> T3["if address != null"] --> T4["getCity()"]
    end
    subgraph Optional
        O1["getUser(id) -> Optional"] --> O2["map(User::getAddress)"] --> O3["map(Address::getCity)"] --> O4["orElse('Unknown')"]
    end
```

**Step-by-step**
1. The traditional approach nests null checks.
2. Optional chains transformations with `map`.
3. `orElse` provides a safe default.

**Architectural reasoning**
- Optional makes null handling explicit and composable.
- Chains are easier to read and less error-prone.
- Avoid Optional for fields; use it for return types and APIs.

```java
// Repository returns Optional
public Optional<User> findByEmail(String email) {
    return userRepository.findByEmail(email);
}

// Service layer chaining
public String getUserCity(String userId) {
    return userRepository.findById(userId)
        .map(User::getAddress)             // User → Address (null-safe)
        .filter(a -> a.isVerified())       // only verified addresses
        .map(Address::getCity)             // Address → city string
        .map(String::toUpperCase)          // transform
        .orElse("UNKNOWN");                // safe default
}

// ❌ Anti-patterns to avoid
optional.get();                     // May throw NoSuchElementException
optional.isPresent() ? opt.get() : default;  // Verbose — use orElse instead
Optional<Optional<User>> nested;    // Never nest Optionals!
```
